segments.text: If your interviewer ever asks, "What is your greatest weakness?"... do not tell the truth.
Do not shake their hand too hard. Do not tell them where you live. And never say you have no questions.
This is Protocol four zero four.
There are four rules. Follow them exactly. Otherwise, you will have to activate the emergency protocol.
Rule one. Do not shake too hard.
The one on the left stands up and holds out his hand. His fingers are longer than they should be.
Everyone told you the same thing. A firm handshake. Show them you are strong.
Do not. In that room, a firm grip is a challenge. And they always answer a challenge.
Squeeze, and he squeezes back. A little harder. Then harder. He does not stop when you stop.
A candidate once gave him the firmest handshake of his life. They heard it from the waiting room.
He signs everything with his left hand now.
So keep your hand soft. Let him hold it. Count to three.
He loses interest, and lets go. He writes something down. "Not a threat." That is a good sign.
Rule two. Do not tell the truth.
Everything you say in that room goes into a file. And the file is a map. A map to you.
"Tell me about yourself." Say your name. Say one sentence about your last job. Then stop.
Never say you live alone. A candidate once did. The one in the middle wrote it down. Then he underlined it. Twice.
Living alone means no one will notice when you stop coming home.
Then he leans forward. "What is your greatest weakness?"
Do not tell the truth. Your real weakness is how they will come for you.
One candidate said, "I'm afraid of the dark." That night, the power went out in his building. Only his building.
Give them the answer everyone gives. "I work too hard." "I'm a perfectionist."
It is already in every file they have. They learn nothing new.
Rule three. Never say you have no questions.
At the end, they put their pens down. "Do you have any questions for us?"
In this room, the interview only ends when you ask something.
Say, "No, I think you covered everything," and look at the clock. It goes back to nine.
The one on the left stands up and holds out his hand again. "Thanks for coming in." It starts over.
It will keep starting over. Every handshake. Every question. Until you ask one.
One candidate said no forty times. For him, it is still Monday, nine A.M.
Do not ask about the salary. Do not ask what happened to the last person in this job.
Ask only this. "When will I hear back?"
They stand up. "We'll be in touch."
Rule four. Emergency protocol. How to fight back.
If you broke even one rule, they will be in touch. Exactly as promised.
Three A.M. You wake up. Three interviewers are standing at the foot of your bed, holding your file.
"We have a few more questions."
Here is what does not work.
Pretending to be asleep. They write down, "Lacks enthusiasm."
Screaming. They write down, "Strong communication skills."
Saying you already took another job. They ask for the company's name. Then they visit that company too.
There is only one thing that works. Remember what they really are. They are not monsters. They are employees.
And every employee is afraid of the same thing.
Sit up. Fold your hands. Look straight at the middle one. "Congratulations. You're hired."
They freeze. In that room, whoever makes the offer is the boss. You just made the offer.
Their folders drop. They stand up straight. They are your employees now.
Then say the words every employee fears. "Unfortunately... we're letting you go. Effective immediately."
Three small cardboard boxes appear in their hands. Inside each one, a stapler and a sad little plant.
They walk out of your bedroom one by one, and you never give them a reference.
The next morning, one new email. "We are sorry to hear about the recent changes in our team."
"We have restructured our hiring process."
Then the doorbell rings. Through the peephole, three new interviewers. One of them is already holding out his hand.
"Welcome to the second round."
And that was Protocol four zero four.
If this ever happens to you... you know the protocol.
